abstract_experiment: Across ViT-Tiny, ViT-Small and ViT-Base (5M–85M parameters, each trained for 50 epochs with and without 4 registers) we find no high-norm tokens at all: the largest token in the last block is at most 2.64× the median, and the registers receive only the attention an average token would get (5.7–6.2% against 5.8%). Registers change accuracy by less than one point (−0.81, +0.44, −0.66). Together with the DINOv2 results, where clear outliers appear only in the 1.1B-parameter ViT-g, this supports the paper’s view that artifacts, and the need for registers, arise only in large, long-trained models. Along the way we found that a shared learning rate of 10<super>−3</super> breaks ViT-Base, so the experiment uses 2.5×10<super>−4</super> for every size.
discussion: Do artifacts appear with model size? Not at the sizes we can train. None of our six models has a single outlier token in its last block, where the paper measures them, and the norm histograms have a single hump (Figure 6), unlike the two humps of DINOv2 ViT-g (Figure 1). The only tokens above 3× the median in any block are about 3–6 of 128,000 in the first two blocks of ViT-Tiny, and they are gone by the third block: the opposite of the paper’s artifacts, which appear in the middle of the network and persist to the output (paper Fig. 4a). On the shared size axis (Figure 4), clear outliers appear only at the very top, in DINOv2 ViT-g, with a small tail in DINOv2 ViT-B.

Why not? Our ViT-Base has the same size as DINOv2 ViT-B, but it saw 100,000 images of 64×64 pixels for 50 epochs instead of 142 million full-size images. The paper reports that high-norm tokens need both a large model and long training (its Fig. 4b and 4c). Our models are therefore below the point where a model has learned enough to treat background patches as redundant and reuse them. Our experiment changes model size but not training length, so it cannot say which of the two matters more; it does show that size alone, up to 85M parameters, is not enough.

What do registers do in a model without artifacts? Almost nothing. Patch tokens give the four registers 6.0%, 5.7% and 6.2% of their last-block attention in Tiny, Small and Base, and [CLS] gives them 6.1–7.6%; uniform attention would give them 5.8%. Their norms are close to those of a typical patch (ViT-Base: 79–98 against a median patch of 96). In DINOv2 ViT-g with registers, by contrast, one register has a norm of 1390 against 108 for a typical patch. This is the clearest evidence in our project for the paper’s explanation: registers are only used as scratch space when the model needs scratch space.

Accuracy. Adding registers changes validation accuracy by −0.81 (Tiny), +0.44 (Small) and −0.66 (Base) points. The paper reports −0.1 to +0.5 points on ImageNet. Our differences are all under a point and have no consistent sign; with one seed per setting we read them as no clear effect, while a small cost cannot be ruled out. Larger models were only marginally more accurate (39.74%, 39.69%, 40.44% without registers) because they memorise the training set (97–99% training accuracy).

The learning rate mattered more than size or registers. With the learning rate of our first ViT-Tiny runs (10−3), ViT-Base collapsed after the warm-up (validation accuracy fell from 12.7% to about 4% and ended below 11%), its token norms grew to about 10,000, and ViT-Small with registers trained so much worse than without registers that the register comparison showed −2.75 points (Table 3, Figure 8). Measuring those models would have produced a misleading result, so we retrained all six models at 2.5×10−4. This is a useful lesson for any size comparison: the training recipe has to work for the largest model before differences between models mean anything.
conclusion: We reproduced the paper’s central diagnosis on the models it studied: in DINOv2 ViT-g, 2.62% of patch tokens have a very large norm (paper: 2.37%); they sit on redundant background patches; registers remove them and clean up the attention maps; and the large values move into the registers. A practical detail the paper does not stress is that these norms are only visible before the model’s final LayerNorm. The model-size claim is only partly reproduced on the released checkpoints, most likely because Meta’s smaller released models were distilled from ViT-g.

Our own ViT with registers, written from scratch, trains normally, and registers change its accuracy by under a point. Our experiment shows that ViTs of 5M–85M parameters trained from scratch on Tiny-ImageNet develop no high-norm artifacts, and that their registers then stay idle, receiving only chance-level attention. This supports the paper’s explanation that registers are scratch space a model only needs once it is large and trained long enough. The deployed FastAPI app makes the effect visible on any photo. Next steps would be longer training or more data to find where artifacts first appear, several seeds per setting, and tests of the paper’s downstream claims (linear probing, LOST object discovery) on the released models.

slide_experiment_notes: This is the main result of our experiment. On the left, the share of outlier tokens; on the right, the largest token divided by the median. Circles are our own models, triangles are Meta's DINOv2. All six of our models, from 5 to 85 million parameters, stay at zero outliers, and the largest token never reaches the 3x line in the last block. Clear outliers only appear at the top of the axis, in DINOv2 giant. Our Base model has the same size as DINOv2 Base, but it saw 100 thousand small images for 50 epochs instead of 142 million images, and the paper says artifacts need both size and long training. So our answer is: at the sizes we can train, the artifacts do not appear.
slide_registers_notes: Inside our models: on the left, the largest-to-median norm after every block stays below 3 for all models. On the right, accuracy and register use. The registers get about 6 percent of the attention, which is what four tokens out of 69 would get by chance, so the model does not really use them. In DINOv2 giant, one register has a norm 13 times a normal patch. Accuracy changes by less than one point with registers, with no consistent sign. One more lesson: with our first learning rate of 1e-3, ViT-Base collapsed, so we retrained all six models at 2.5e-4 before comparing.
